blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the challenge of trust and interpretability in reinforcement learning (RL) controllers, especially for real-world deployments and human-machine collaborations. The paper introduces Programmatically Interpretable Reinforcement Learning (PIRL), which addresses this by defining a domain-specific language (DSL) for expressing policies as interpretable programs. The key insight is to constrain the search space of possible programs using a 'sketch' (a program template) and guide the search with a black-box RL policy (the Neural Policy Oracle). The Neurally Directed Program Search (NDPS) algorithm then finds a program that mimics the oracle's behavior while remaining interpretable. Colyer notes that while the interpretable model may not match the oracle's performance on training tasks, it often generalizes better to new situations, likely due to reduced overfitting. The paper demonstrates PIRL's effectiveness in learning human-readable policies for tasks like driving a race car in TORCS, with smoother trajectories and better transferability compared to deep RL methods.
paper_abstract: We present a reinforcement learning framework, called Programmatically Interpretable Reinforcement Learning (P IRL), that is designed to generate interpretable and verifiable agent policies. Unlike the popular Deep Reinforcement Learning (D RL) paradigm, which represents policies by neural networks, P IRL represents policies using a high-level, domain-specific programming language. Such programmatic policies have the benefits of being more easily interpreted than neural networks, and being amenable to verification by symbolic methods. We propose a new method, called Neurally Directed Program Search (N DPS), for solving the challenging nonsmooth optimization problem of finding a programmatic policy with maximal reward. N DPS works by first learning a neural policy network using D RL, and then performing a local search over programmatic policies that seeks to minimize a distance from this neural “oracle”. We evaluate N DPS on the task of learning to drive a simulated car in the T ORCS carracing environment. We demonstrate that N DPS is able to discover human-readable policies that pass some significant performance bars. We also show that P IRL policies can have smoother trajectories, and can be more easily transferred to environments not encountered during training, than corresponding policies discovered by D RL.
